migrationNotes: Spine: a colleague asks for a trimmed view of the shop's orders, and we reshape one table three times (fewer columns, a new heading, a calculated column) while the stored table stays whole.
Left out of the lesson (still in the course): sql-select-and-name-8 (which query returns only the id column; its syntax is taught on the first screen and tested again in the skill check)

lesson.title: Choose the columns you need

lead.text: The shop's orders table has six columns, and most questions about it need only a few of them. Asking a database for something is called writing a query, and the simplest query has two parts. SELECT lists the columns you want, separated by commas. FROM names the table to read them from.

So SELECT id, item FROM orders asks for the id and the item of every order, and nothing else. The answer is a new, smaller grid called the result, built at the moment you ask. Use the buttons under the picture to compare asking for everything with asking for two columns.

afterFigure.text: A star in place of the list means every column, so SELECT * FROM orders gives the whole table back. The result has the same six rows either way. SELECT decides which columns appear, and the rows come along unchanged.

queries.label: Every column
queries.sql: SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Id and item
queries.sql: SELECT id, item FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: Each name in the list after SELECT becomes one column of the result.

Think back to the colleague's request. Hiding the columns left your own sheet complete, and a query treats a table the same way. It reads the stored table and builds a separate result from it. Whatever you ask for, the table behind the result keeps all of its columns and all of its rows.

That is what makes asking safe. One person can ask for two columns while another asks for five, and neither changes what the other sees. If you leave out a column you turn out to need, you ask again with a longer list, because the column was never gone.
The result is a copy built for one question, so you can reshape it as much as you like. The next two screens do exactly that, first by changing a heading and then by working out a new column.
Hiding a column in a shared view takes it out of the view only.

The columns of a result normally carry the table's own names, but those names aren't always the ones a reader wants. Your colleague might call the amount column price. You can ask for that by writing AS after the column, as in SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders. The word after AS is an alias, a name that column goes by in this result.
Compare the two queries in the picture. They return the same ids and the same numbers, and the second one labels its second column price.

afterFigure.text: Only the heading in the result changes. Every amount is the same as before, and the table still calls its column amount, so the next query can use that name again. An alias is a label on the copy you were handed, and nothing stored is renamed.

queries.label: Without AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: With AS
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: The query SELECT id, amount AS price FROM orders adds an alias.

steps.headline: A column worked out from others

lead.text: A column in the result doesn't have to be copied straight from the table. After SELECT you can write an expression, which is a small calculation made from a row's own values. Take amount / 2, for example. The database works it out separately for each row and puts the answers in the result, and AS gives the new column a heading, as in amount / 2 AS half.

An unknown value stays unknown. Half of a missing amount is still missing, so a NULL goes in and a NULL comes out. The picture sets the original amounts beside the halved ones, and order 106 shows it.

afterFigure.text: The expression uses the usual signs for adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing, which are +, −, * and /. Changing the expression changes the question the result answers. Halving scales every amount, while adding ten shifts every amount by the same sum. Each answer comes from that row's own values, and the stored table is never touched.

queries.label: Original amounts
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount FROM orders ORDER BY id;

queries.label: Halve each amount
queries.sql: SELECT id, amount / 2 AS half FROM orders ORDER BY id;

lead.text: A SELECT list can hold an expression, and it is worked out once for every row.
Changing the expression changes the question. Doubling scales each amount, and this query adds a fixed sum instead.

lesson.orientation: Use SELECT and aliases to shape a result without changing the stored table.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A colleague asks for the shop's orders, so you open the spreadsheet. It has six columns of facts about each order, and your colleague only wants to compare prices. You hide every column except three and send them that view.

Nothing has been deleted. Your colleague sees three columns, and your own sheet still has all six, ready for the next person who wants something different. People reshape a sheet like this all the time before they share it. They hide columns, give a column a friendlier heading, or add a column that works something out from the others.

A database does the same when you ask it for a new view of a table. This lesson takes the shop's orders table through each of those changes in turn. The table itself never changes, and every answer is a fresh result built next to it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll shape a query result with SELECT, AS and simple expressions, knowing the stored table never changes.

recap.keyIdea: SELECT shapes the result with the columns and expressions you list. AS labels them, and the stored table stays exactly as it was.

blocks.text: Back with your colleague's request, you counted 2 result columns, saw that hiding columns leaves all 6 in the sheet, and worked out 160 for a doubled amount of 80 and 30 for 10 added to 20. The orders table never changed.

recap.nextHook: Every query so far has returned all six orders, whatever columns it showed. A bookshop sign that covers only some of the books on the shelf begins the following lesson, which is about keeping just the rows that pass a test.

questions.prompt: How many columns does SELECT id, amount FROM orders return?
hints: Count the names in the list after SELECT.
Rows and columns measure different things, and this question asks about columns.
The list is id, amount. Count each name once.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The SELECT list names id and amount: two columns.

questions.onCorrect: 2. Each name in the SELECT list is one column of the result. The rows are unchanged.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every column of the table. The list names only some of them.
The list has two names, separated by a comma.

questions.prompt: A query contains amount AS price. What does the AS part change?
hints: An alias belongs to the result.

acceptedIdeas: The heading in the query result
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AS price labels the column in this query's result. It does not rename the stored amount column.

choices.label: The heading in the query result

questions.onCorrect: The heading in the result. The alias labels the output and leaves the stored column alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The stored values stay as they were. AS only affects how the result is labelled.
Aliases never add or remove rows. They only label a column.

questions.prompt: A query works out amount * 2 for every order. What does it give for order 101, whose amount is 80?
hints: Apply the expression to this one row's amount.
Multiply 80 by two.
Evaluate 80 × 2. The alias, if there is one, only names the column.
questions.onCorrect: 160. The expression is worked out for each row; AS only names the new column.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2. The expression multiplies by 2.
That is the stored amount. The expression changes the value in the result.

questions.prompt: A query works out amount + 10 for every order. What does it give for order 102, whose amount is 20?
hints: This expression adds a fixed amount.
Add ten to twenty.
Evaluate 20 + 10; multiplication is not part of this expression.
questions.onCorrect: 30. This expression adds a fixed amount to each row, so a different question gets a different answer.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles the amount. This expression adds 10.

questions.prompt: An amount is 15. What would SELECT amount * 3 AS tripled return for that row?
hints: AS names the column; the multiplication produces the value.
Multiply fifteen by three.
Evaluate 15 × 3, keeping the alias separate from the value.
questions.onCorrect: 45. Multiply 15 by 3; the alias tripled is only the heading.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3. The expression multiplies by 3.
That is the amount before the expression is applied.

questions.prompt: After SELECT amount AS price, type the column name that remains in the stored table.
hints: SELECT reads the table; this alias does not alter its schema.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The stored column remains amount. The alias price belongs to the query result, so another query can still refer to amount.

questions.onCorrect: amount. The alias exists only in the result, so another query can still use the stored name.

misconceptions.feedback: price is the heading in this query's result. The table itself was never renamed.

questions.prompt: You hide every column of a six-column spreadsheet except three, then send that view to a colleague. How many columns does your original sheet still have?
hints: Does hiding a column delete it?
The sheet you started with keeps everything it had.
Count the columns you started with, including the ones now hidden.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hiding changes only what is shown. The original sheet keeps all six columns.

questions.onCorrect: 6. Hiding columns changes the view you share, not the sheet it came from. A query result works the same way.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number you chose to show. The original sheet still has the hidden ones too.

questions.prompt: Which query returns only the id column of orders?
hints: The column list comes straight after SELECT.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: SELECT id FROM orders; lists id after SELECT and names the table after FROM.

questions.onCorrect: SELECT lists the columns you want, then FROM names the table they come from.

misconceptions.feedback: The star asks for every column, not just one.
The words are in the wrong order. SELECT starts the query, and FROM follows the column list.

questions.prompt: An order has amount 12. What does SELECT amount - 5 AS reduced return for that row?
hints: Which part is the calculation and which part is the name?
AS only names the result column.
Take 5 off 12.
questions.onCorrect: 7. The expression does the calculation and AS only names the column it appears in.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 5. The expression subtracts it.
